artworks.title: Nestor Appearing in a Dream to Agamemnon
artworks.description: Engraving by James Heath after Henry Fuseli, held in the British Museum, illustrating the opening of Homer's Iliad (Book II). Here Zeus dispatches one of the Oneiroi, the personified Dreams born of Night, to the sleeping Agamemnon. The Dream-spirit assumes the shape of the aged counsellor Nestor and leans over the Greek king's couch to whisper the deceitful message that the gods have decreed Troy's fall, urging him to arm. Fuseli renders the Oneiros as a looming, shadowy apparition hovering at the bedside, capturing the dream-gods' twin nature as both messengers and deceivers of mortal sleep.

artworks.title: Morpheus Awakening as Iris Draws Near
artworks.description: Oil on canvas by Rene-Antoine Houasse, commissioned in 1688 for the Chamber of Sleep at the Grand Trianon, Palace of Versailles. The painting shows the rainbow-goddess Iris descending on a cloud to the cavern of Sleep, where she rouses Morpheus, chief of the Oneiroi, the dream-shaping sons of Somnus. The scene follows Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book XI): at Juno's bidding Iris orders Morpheus to take on the likeness of the drowned Ceyx and visit his widow Alcyone in a dream. Houasse presents the Oneiros as a winged, languid youth surrounded by sleeping putti, the classic Baroque image of a dream-god summoned to his nightly errand.

artworks.title: Morpheus, in the Form of Ceyx, Appears to Alcyone
artworks.description: Engraving by the Nuremberg master Virgil Solis from his illustrated edition of Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book XI, lines 650-749). The print depicts Morpheus, the foremost of the Oneiroi and the dream-spirit who counterfeits human forms, appearing in a vision to the sleeping Alcyone. Sent at Juno's command, the Oneiros has taken on the dripping, death-pale shape of her husband Ceyx, drowned at sea, to break the news of his death. Solis condenses the dream into a single chamber scene, the spectral Oneiros bending over the dreaming queen, embodying the dream-gods' power to wear the faces of the living and the dead.
